newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German film industry revived after years of decline.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German film industry revived after years of decline.

text.p: Germany's film industry has emerged from years in the doldrums with a string of powerful box office hits, raising hopes that it can recapture some of the international cinematic allure ruined by the Nazis and decades of dull post-war pictures.

Rejuvenated by a run of popular romantic comedies made for large mainstream audiences rather than tiny art house crowds, German films produced more hits in 1996 than ever before and grabbed a market share at home of 17 percent.

Although modest by some standards, this was nearly double the level of 1995 and a widely applauded result for a market that watched with dismay as Hollywood dominated with a share of 80 to 90 percent for decades.

"German films did exceptionally well last year," said Frank Voelkert, director of the German Film Federation in Berlin. "More people saw German films than in any single year since the 1960s. The industry is making commercially successful films that the public wants to see."

Five German-made films pulled in box office receipts of more than 12 million marks ($7.5 million) and one German film, "Werner", grossed 50 million marks. Three of the country's top ten grossing films last year were German-made.
With fast-paced and well-written scripts, the new genre of films focus on issues that interest Germans such as such as faithless partners, sexual orientation, and women's liberation.
NEW FILMS REFLECT LIBERAL EUROPE
They lack the occasional prudishness of Hollywood pictures and generally reflect the morals of liberal northern European audiences rather than southern California.
German films, for example, are far more open in their portrayal of homosexuality than Hollywood.
"German audiences are enjoying seeing films about the subjects that more directly affect their lives," said Dirk Dotzert, editor of the weekly magazine "Blickpunkt Film."

"There are many good stories being well presented by an industry that has gained in professionalism in recent years," he added. "There is a whole new generation of film makers on the scene making films for the audiences, not themselves."

The best and brightest examples of Germany's film industry will be shown at the 47th annual Berlin Film Festival that opens on Thursday and runs until February 24. The Berlinale is considered Europe's second most prestigious festival after Cannes, which is held in May.

The increasing glamour of the Berlinale, which has become an important stop for Hollywood producers, directors and actors in recent years, has also contributed to the local optimism of restoring some of the pre-war film glitter to Germany.
BERLIN'S PRE-WAR CINEMATIC FAME

Before the Nazis took power in 1933, the Babelsberg studio outside Berlin was one of the world's leading film centres, producing classics like Fritz Lang's "Metropolis" in 1926 and Josef von Sternberg's "Der Blaue Engel" (The Blue Angel), starring Marlene Dietrich, in 1930.

But Lang, Dietrich, Billy Wilder and others left for Hollywood and what was left of the local film industry was misused by the Nazis for propaganda. After the war, dull auteur films often written, directed, produced and starred the same person helped bury the industry further.
With unification in 1990, Germany and its population of 80 million became the world's second largest film market with annual sales of 1.3 billion marks. It trails only the U.S.
While Hollywood still dominates the German and most foreign markets, the sharp gains in Germany have not gone unnoticed.

Many major Hollywood studios such as Buena Vista, Columbia Tri-Star and Warner Brothers have got into the local act by distributing and, in some cases, even producing, German-language films for the local market.

That is not without risks because the German-language market, which amounts to less than 100 million if Austria and Switzerland are included, is still considerably smaller than the vast English-language audience potential.

"It is hopefully only a matter of time before the domestic success can be turned into export success as well," said Christian Dorsch, head of the German Film Export Union. But he admitted that even the most successful German films will have a hard time breaking into major markets in the United States, France, Britain, Italy and Spain.

U.S. and British audiences tend to eschew films with subtitles or dubbing and the European markets have proved equally hard to penetrate, although the 1995 hit "Der Bewegte Mann" (Maybe...Maybe Not) earned more than 70 million marks in Germany and had extensive foreign sales.

The Disney subsidiary Buena Vista earned more than 17 million marks with one hit comedy "Irren ist Maennlich" (To Err is Human) and another 10 million marks with a widely acclaimed drama "Jenseits der Stille" (The Quiet Side).
Though the revenues may be modest by Hollywood standards, they are exceptional for Germany, where as early as 1991 not a single film had box office revenues of over four million marks.

The films were also profitable for the studio because comparatively inexpensive film making in Germany means that it rarely costs more than three million marks to make a feature length film -- a fraction of the cost of most Hollywood films.
"The market share of German films will certainly continue to expand in the years ahead," said Wolfgang Braun, director of Buena Vista's German operations.

"We have already seen the tastes of German television viewers switch to the point that there are almost no more American series on prime time. A similar trend, although not as extreme, will likely hit the film market as well."

A decade ago, American-made series and made for TV movies dominated the country's prime time evening line-up. Today, there are Dallas-like soap operas -- but they are German-made productions with Berliners or Bavarians rather than Texans.
